summary: A proposal by John Day for a File Access Protocol, an extension of FTP that lets a program work with remote files more like a local file system. Day offers it as a starting point and asks for comments, including on holey Tenex files and record-oriented systems.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 520 proposes an FTP extension that lets a program choose where to read or write in a remote file. This can transfer only the data the program needs instead of the whole file.

questions: what is the file access protocol
what is a file pointer in ftp
how does the fap file pointer work
subtitle: A proposed FTP extension for reading or writing selected parts of a remote file.

tldr.problem: A process that needs only part of a remote file may otherwise have to transfer the entire file.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed File Access Protocol extends FTP with a file pointer and six commands for opening a file, moving the pointer, reading or writing data, and closing the file.
tldr.outcome: RFC 520 presents FAP as a proposal for comment. Its author says he would eventually like to merge the commands into FTP.

today: The unit records RFC 520's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It presents FAP as a proposal and invites comments on its design and implementation.

sections.title: Accessing Parts of Remote Files
sections.content:
The File Access Protocol (FAP) is proposed as an extension to FTP. It lets a process access a non-local file sequentially or non-sequentially by specifying where an operation should start and how much data to move. The stated aim is to avoid transferring and storing parts of a file that the process does not need.

FAP uses FTP's connection model, data representations and transmission methods, with changes to mark the end of an access. In stream mode, the minimum byte size is increased to four bits and control code value 4 indicates end of transmission. In block mode, bit 5 of the descriptor marks the final block.
sections.plainLanguage: FAP lets a program point to a place in a remote file and request data from there. It uses FTP's existing transfer methods with extra signals for ending an access.

sections.title: Limits on What Hosts Must Support
sections.content:
The proposal does not require a host to offer network users file access that it does not provide to its local users. Some systems may support random access only for certain files, may not move a pointer backward without reopening a file, or may not support reading and writing in the same open session.

The RFC says an operation should be allowed when the system normally permits it for that kind of file. Hosts should not simulate a feature when doing so has side effects, and implementors should document their capabilities in NIC documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A host only needs to offer file operations that its own system can support. It should document its limits instead of pretending to provide a feature that could cause side effects.

sections.title: The File Pointer
sections.content:
FAP's file pointer identifies where the next read or write begins. It counts logical bytes, excluding transmission and structure markers, and takes the value B for the beginning, E for the end, or a number from the file. The meaning of a logical byte accounts for local data transformations described by the RFC.

SETP moves the pointer and GETP reports its position. An attempt to move it to an unsupported position can receive reply 402; a request beyond the end can receive an EOF reply with the end position.
sections.plainLanguage: The file pointer marks where the next operation starts. It can identify the beginning, the end or a position within the file.

sections.title: Opening, Reading, Writing and Closing
sections.content:
OPEN selects a file and read, write or both directions; it places the pointer at the beginning. READ transfers a specified number of bytes or ALL from server to user. WRIT accepts that amount from user to server and updates the pointer. A request may stop at the end of the file or record, with a reply identifying that boundary.

CLOS closes the currently open file; sending it when no file is open is not an error. The cover note observes that an OPEN, READ ALL, CLOS sequence can do the same as an FTP RETR for a whole file.
sections.plainLanguage: Open a file, set the pointer, and read or write the amount needed. Close the file when done; FAP also allows more than one access without closing the connection each time.
